Q: Which solid materials have been burned in Moon-base air, at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less?

Two solid materials have been burned in Moon-base air at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less: SIBAL Cloth and Two-Sided PMMA [2]. Saffire VI-2 burned SIBAL Cloth at 31.0 mol % oxygen and 54.1 kPa ambient pressure, and Saffire VI-3 burned Two-Sided PMMA at 30.3 mol % oxygen and 54.6 kPa ambient pressure, both at 20 cm/s air flow [2]. ABOUT
Known Limits
What this site and its sources cannot tell you, so nothing on a chart implies more than the sources say. Grouped by part of the site; open a group, or expand all.
The headline
It counts solid-material tests only, and only those in our sources (PSI downloads plus 6 cited papers and pages). We do not claim to have seen every test ever run.

The 2 tests inside the Moon-base zone (Saffire VI-2, SIBAL Cloth; Saffire VI-3, Two-Sided PMMA) ran at 20 cm/s airflow, in microgravity. None ran in partial gravity: "there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI" (challenge page).
Two tests are not a flammability boundary. They show that these materials burned under those conditions, not where they stop burning.

ABOUT
Fire safety on Earth

The challenge page names these Earth uses of NASA fire-safety work. For each: the page's words, the NASA source it links, and the PSI investigations on the same topic, each with a quote from its own PSI metadata. A shared topic is not a claim of origin.
SUPPRESSION Fine-water-mist fire extinguishers 3 related PSI investigations
DETECTION Smoke detector that tells smoke from dust 4 related PSI investigations
FIREFIGHTER GEAR Firefighters' air tanks and breathing gear no PSI link in our sources
FIREFIGHTER GEAR Firefighter protective clothing no PSI link in our sources
Suppression
Fine-water-mist fire extinguishers
"Fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for use on the ISS have practical applications here on Earth" challenge page
Source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page challenge page
0 of 24 PSI combustion investigations mention water mist in their metadata. The investigations listed studied suppression in other ways (gases, models).
Related PSI investigations

PSI-69 Flame Extinguishment Experiment · DOI Suppression agents tested in microgravity (gases, not water mist): "measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6" Comment[Objective] · L71

PSI-69 Flame Extinguishment Experiment · DOI FLEX's own statement of Earth benefit: "can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems" Comment[Research Impacts] · L78

PSI-26 Burning and Suppression of Solids · DOI Suppression of burning solids by nitrogen dilution: "Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques." Comment[Research Impacts] · L69

PSI-25 Burning and Suppression of Solids - II · DOI Models used to design suppression systems, including on Earth: "BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth." Comment[Objective] · L60
Detection
Smoke detector that tells smoke from dust
"NASA technology has similarly led to improvements in terrestrial smoke detection" challenge page

Source: Fire Detector (NASA Spinoff): "1970s smoke detector developed for the shuttle that, discriminating between smoke and dust, results in less nuisance alarms. As such, it has industrial applications (e.g., in mining operations)." challenge page Resources tab
The challenge page's resource note dates this to the 1970s. The investigations below share its topic; we do not claim they led to it.

The challenge page links the two: "One of the instruments used for smoke detection in the SAME and SAME-R studies was instead used to detect dust in the Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT and DAFT-2) studies."
Related PSI investigations

PSI-102 Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment · DOI How smoke detectors respond to smoke made in microgravity: "affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke" Comment[Hypothesis] · L48

PSI-101 Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight · DOI SAME-R's own statement of Earth benefit: "can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories" Comment[Research Impacts] · L67

PSI-47 Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 · DOI Dust measured with a smoke-detection instrument: the smoke-versus-dust problem: "Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard" Comment[Approach] · L40

PSI-115 Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity · DOI Ground analysis of SAME data: "This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices" Comment[Research Impacts] · L65
Firefighter gear
Firefighters' air tanks and breathing gear
"firefighter gear, including protective clothing and air tanks" challenge page
Source: Fireman's Air Tanks (NASA Spinoff): "1970s adaptation of spacesuit technology to improve firefighters' air tanks and breathing gear." challenge page Resources tab
The challenge page's resource note dates this to the 1970s.
No PSI combustion investigation is linked to this in our sources. The resource note describes it as an adaptation of spacesuit technology.

What this site and its sources cannot tell you, so nothing on a chart implies more than the sources say. Grouped by part of the site; open a group, or expand all.
The headline
It counts solid-material tests only, and only those in our sources (PSI downloads plus 6 cited papers and pages). We do not claim to have seen every test ever run.

The 2 tests inside the Moon-base zone (Saffire VI-2, SIBAL Cloth; Saffire VI-3, Two-Sided PMMA) ran at 20 cm/s airflow, in microgravity. None ran in partial gravity: "there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI" (challenge page).
Two tests are not a flammability boundary. They show that these materials burned under those conditions, not where they stop burning.

Fire safety on Earth

The challenge page names these Earth uses of NASA fire-safety work. For each: the page's words, the NASA source it links, and the PSI investigations on the same topic, each with a quote from its own PSI metadata. A shared topic is not a claim of origin.
SUPPRESSION Fine-water-mist fire extinguishers 3 related PSI investigations
DETECTION Smoke detector that tells smoke from dust 4 related PSI investigations
FIREFIGHTER GEAR Firefighters' air tanks and breathing gear no PSI link in our sources
FIREFIGHTER GEAR Firefighter protective clothing no PSI link in our sources
Suppression
Fine-water-mist fire extinguishers
"Fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for use on the ISS have practical applications here on Earth" challenge page
Source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page challenge page
0 of 24 PSI combustion investigations mention water mist in their metadata. The investigations listed studied suppression in other ways (gases, models).
Related PSI investigations

PSI-69 Flame Extinguishment Experiment · DOI Suppression agents tested in microgravity (gases, not water mist): "measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6" Comment[Objective] · L71

PSI-69 Flame Extinguishment Experiment · DOI FLEX's own statement of Earth benefit: "can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems" Comment[Research Impacts] · L78

PSI-26 Burning and Suppression of Solids · DOI Suppression of burning solids by nitrogen dilution: "Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques." Comment[Research Impacts] · L69

PSI-25 Burning and Suppression of Solids - II · DOI Models used to design suppression systems, including on Earth: "BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth." Comment[Objective] · L60
Detection
Smoke detector that tells smoke from dust
"NASA technology has similarly led to improvements in terrestrial smoke detection" challenge page

Source: Fire Detector (NASA Spinoff): "1970s smoke detector developed for the shuttle that, discriminating between smoke and dust, results in less nuisance alarms. As such, it has industrial applications (e.g., in mining operations)." challenge page Resources tab
The challenge page's resource note dates this to the 1970s. The investigations below share its topic; we do not claim they led to it.

The challenge page links the two: "One of the instruments used for smoke detection in the SAME and SAME-R studies was instead used to detect dust in the Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT and DAFT-2) studies."
Related PSI investigations

PSI-102 Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment · DOI How smoke detectors respond to smoke made in microgravity: "affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke" Comment[Hypothesis] · L48

PSI-101 Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight · DOI SAME-R's own statement of Earth benefit: "can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories" Comment[Research Impacts] · L67

PSI-47 Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 · DOI Dust measured with a smoke-detection instrument: the smoke-versus-dust problem: "Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard" Comment[Approach] · L40

PSI-115 Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity · DOI Ground analysis of SAME data: "This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices" Comment[Research Impacts] · L65
